# Proof

We use the Cauchy completeness of the real numbers: every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges to a real number. (This is the completeness fact supplied by the standard construction of \(\mathbb R\); without some completeness property, the assertion does not follow merely from the ordered-field axioms, as \(\mathbb Q\) shows.)

We first record the resulting nested-interval lemma. Suppose
\[
I_n=[a_n,b_n]\qquad(n=0,1,2,\ldots)
\]
are nonempty closed intervals such that \(I_{n+1}\subseteq I_n\) and \(b_n-a_n\to0\). Then \((a_n)\) is Cauchy. Indeed, if \(m\ge n\), nesting gives
\[
a_n\le a_m\le b_n,
\]
so \(0\le a_m-a_n\le b_n-a_n\). Thus, once \(n\) is sufficiently large, this difference is arbitrarily small; interchanging the two indices handles every pair of sufficiently large indices. By Cauchy completeness, \(a_n\to x\) for some \(x\in\mathbb R\). For each fixed \(n\), all \(a_m\) with \(m\ge n\) lie in the closed interval \([a_n,b_n]\), and hence their limit \(x\) lies there as well. Therefore \(x\in I_n\) for every \(n\). Moreover, if \(x,z\in I_n\) for every \(n\), then \(|x-z|\le b_n-a_n\) for every \(n\), and taking \(n\to\infty\) gives \(x=z\). Hence the nested intervals have exactly one common point.

Now let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R\) be nonempty and bounded above. Choose \(s_0\in S\), and choose an upper bound \(U\) of \(S\). Put
\[
a_0=s_0-1,\qquad b_0=U.
\]
Then \(a_0<b_0\), \(a_0\) is not an upper bound of \(S\) (because \(s_0>a_0\)), and \(b_0\) is an upper bound.

Inductively, suppose \(a_n\) is not an upper bound of \(S\) and \(b_n\) is an upper bound. Let
\[
m_n=\frac{a_n+b_n}{2}.
\]
If \(m_n\) is an upper bound of \(S\), set \((a_{n+1},b_{n+1})=(a_n,m_n)\). If it is not, set \((a_{n+1},b_{n+1})=(m_n,b_n)\). In either case, \(a_{n+1}\) is not an upper bound, \(b_{n+1}\) is an upper bound, and
\[
[a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq[a_n,b_n],
\qquad b_{n+1}-a_{n+1}=\frac12(b_n-a_n).
\]
Consequently
\[
b_n-a_n=2^{-n}(b_0-a_0)\longrightarrow0.
\]
By the nested-interval lemma, there is a unique \(x\in\mathbb R\) belonging to every \([a_n,b_n]\).

We show first that \(x\) is an upper bound of \(S\). If some \(s\in S\) satisfied \(s>x\), choose \(n\) so large that \(b_n-a_n<s-x\). Since \(x\in[a_n,b_n]\),
\[
b_n-x\le b_n-a_n<s-x,
\]
and hence \(b_n<s\). This contradicts the fact that \(b_n\) is an upper bound of \(S\). Thus every \(s\in S\) satisfies \(s\le x\).

Finally, let \(y<x\). Choose \(n\) so large that \(b_n-a_n<x-y\). Since \(x\in[a_n,b_n]\),
\[
x-a_n\le b_n-a_n<x-y,
\]
so \(a_n>y\). Because \(a_n\) is not an upper bound of \(S\), there is some \(s\in S\) with \(s>a_n>y\). Therefore no number smaller than \(x\) is an upper bound of \(S\). Since \(x\) itself is an upper bound, it is the least upper bound:
\[
x=\sup S.
\]
Thus every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb R\) that is bounded above admits a supremum in \(\mathbb R\).
